source.title: Bringing Up a Bilingual BabyLM: Investigating Multilingual Language Acquisition Using Small-Scale Models
source.authors: L. Zeng; Steven Y. Feng; Michael C. Frank

record.tranche_reason: The study varies model size and training-data amount and reports downstream semantic and grammatical evaluation outcomes, but it does not fit the original held-out-loss scaling curves or test compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions prior scaling-law research and says its own performance pattern is approximately logarithmic with training-data amount. It does not report fits or numerical held-out-loss scaling curves for parameter count, tokens, or compute. Perplexity values in the main tables compare language-exposure conditions rather than a scaling-law sweep, so they are not recorded as rows for V1–V3. The scale results used here are reported in text with figures; the figure values are not present in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a study of bilingual exposure. In secondary experiments it varies GPT-2 size (16M, 39M, 124M) and data (20M vs 100M words) on small child-directed-speech corpora and reports downstream semantic and grammatical results. That bears weakly on V6 in a new small-scale setting. There are no loss-curve fits, extrapolations or allocation sweeps, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is that bilingual training neither causes interference nor gives advantages over monolingual training, and that exposure regimes matter little. The scale statements are secondary: performance tracked the amount of data per language, 'approximately logarithmic', consistent with Hoffmann et al. That is a qualitative description, not a fit. The null bilingual effects persisted across model sizes and data scales.
record.recipe_differences: Controlled multilingual exposure experiments with GPT-2 models and downstream linguistic evaluations; no scaling-law fitting, large-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data amount affected downstream performance; reducing model size did not decrease performance in the reported Mini comparison and caused only marginal decreases for Tiny.
record.problems: The scale findings are qualitative in the supplied text, with numerical values confined to figures not included here. The tested models are small, and the authors note that their evaluations cover only a subset of capabilities.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the tested version. Main-table perplexity comparisons were not extracted as scaling-law results because they compare exposure conditions rather than fitted parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling curves.

untested.parts: No held-out loss curve over orders of magnitude. The only loss evidence is two perplexity points (50M vs 100M English words).
No fits on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.
Mini and Tiny change depth, heads and width together, so shape is not varied at a fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data or fine-tuning scaling law.
No quantitative prediction of downstream scores from scale or loss, and no fitted curve. Only directional comparisons over a narrow range.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: English downstream scores at 50M vs 100M English words (English Baseline random vs Topline): semantics 0.55 vs 0.58, Zorro 75.41 vs 77.91 (Spanish pair); similar in the Chinese and Dutch pairs.
Varying per-language data share (10–90%) within 100M words. Authors call the performance vs language-data relationship approximately logarithmic, citing Hoffmann et al.; no fit is reported.
English validation perplexity at 50M vs 100M English words (2.69 vs 2.43). Two points only, so a power law cannot be determined.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3. The scale manipulations are side experiments in a new setting (BabyLM-sized, synthetic child-directed dialogue, 20 epochs), not a different method aimed at the scaling question. All scale evidence is directional with two or three points. The Hoffmann et al. reference is cited, not tested.

versions.untested_parts: No test of held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fits or predictions of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or estimate of compute-optimal parameter and token counts.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No test of scaling-law form in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests downstream semantic and grammatical evaluations across model and data scales, but not a quantitative prediction from pretraining loss or a fitted scaling curve.
No test of how scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on fitting choices or setup.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Mini
rows.operation_detail: Reduced model size while holding training data fixed; compared with GPT-2 Small.

conditions.value: English and Chinese semantic and grammatical knowledge

rows.value: Decreasing model size did not decrease performance.
rows.note: The text gives this aggregate result; numerical figure values are not included in the supplied text.
rows.check: State is correct: the text says reducing 124M to 39M 'did not decrease performance' at fixed data. Training ran 20 epochs on about 100M words, so data is plausibly the bottleneck. This is weak evidence against parameter scaling in general. Values are figure-only (Fig. 5).

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Reduced training data from 100M to 20M words.

conditions.value: English and Chinese semantic and grammatical knowledge

rows.value: Reducing data exposure decreased performance across the board.
rows.note: The text reports an aggregate decrease; numerical figure values are not included in the supplied text.
rows.check: Only two data points (20M vs 100M words), so this shows direction only, not predictability. Values are figure-only (Fig. 6).

rows.subject: GPT-2 Tiny
rows.operation_detail: Extended the Spanish model-size comparison to a smaller model.
rows.value: Only marginal performance decreases, with similar relative trends across conditions.
rows.note: The text gives an aggregate description; numerical figure values are not included in the supplied text.
rows.check: 'Only marginal performance decreases' at 16M is a small move in the expected direction, so partial is correct. This is Spanish only (Fig. 7), figure-only.

relationships.condition: Training data reduced from 100M to 20M words (GPT-2 124M; English and Chinese evaluations)
relationships.reason: Reducing data lowered downstream semantic and grammatical performance across the board (r2). Direction only.
relationships.display_finding: Reducing training data from 100M to 20M words lowered downstream semantic and grammatical performance across English and Chinese evaluations.

relationships.condition: Parameter count reduced (124M→39M→16M) at fixed about 100M words of child-directed data
relationships.reason: Downstream scores did not fall at 39M and fell only marginally at 16M (r1, r3). Parameter scale gives little gain in this data-limited small regime.
relationships.display_finding: Reducing parameters from 124M to 39M preserved downstream scores, and reducing them to 16M caused only marginal declines with about 100M training words.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reduced versus full training-data exposure in the reported English and Chinese evaluations
reader_labels.reason: Reducing data exposure lowered downstream performance across the reported evaluations, consistent with better performance at greater data scale (r2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Model-size comparisons with training data held fixed
reader_labels.reason: The study reports no performance decrease when reducing GPT-2 Small to Mini, and only marginal decreases for Tiny, so parameter scaling did not yield a clear, consistent improvement in these evaluations (r1, r3).
